paras: The Kansas City housing dynamitings of 1919 were a series of threats and dynamite attacks in the spring of 1919 against Black residents who had bought homes in white districts of Kansas City, Missouri. Black papers reported that several Black homes were damaged by "unknown enemies," and that on a Tuesday night in mid-May a charge of dynamite damaged New Hope Baptist Church at 19th and Waldron. No one was reported hurt, and the attacks came while a committee appointed by Mayor Cowgill was meeting Black leaders over the dispute.

In January 1919 the Kansas City Sun wrote that for as much as ten years Black families who moved "from the hollows to the hilltops" had had their homes blown up, with little result from police inquiries. By April, Black purchases of homes in certain sections had produced what the Sun called an "acute race problem," with "many threats made and mass meetings held by the white people in the disputed territory." The Kansas City Post, edited by Dr. Burris A. Jenkins, warned that talk of meeting Black expansion "with Ku Klux Klans and dynamite" was "talking anarchy" and called for committees of both races.
Mayor Cowgill then named a white committee chaired by Jenkins, which met a Black committee that included Dr. J. E. Dibble, Rev. William H. Thomas and lawyer C. H. Calloway.

On May 3 a Sun letter writer, Mrs. J. R. Williams, referred to white "Protest Meetings" where measures of violence were discussed to keep Black buyers out of homes they had paid for. In the same issue an editorial brief said that southeast residents had recently taken up a collection to buy dynamite. According to an item from Pearson's Magazine reprinted in the Cleveland Advocate, dynamiting of "the better class of Negro homes" had resumed in Kansas City, and several homes of well-off Black residents had been damaged within a few weeks.

The Sun reported that on the Tuesday night before its May 17 issue a charge of dynamite exploded under the rear wall of New Hope Baptist Church, whose pastor was Rev. S. W. Toles. The paper attributed the blast "presumably" to someone from the element that had been threatening to destroy Black property on the East side. The explosion broke windows in several nearby homes and did more than a hundred dollars' damage to a brick flat south of the church occupied by white people.

Toles notified the police, asked for protection, and said the church would be repaired, a watchman installed and services continued. The four or five Black families in the neighborhood told the Sun they were not frightened and would stay in the homes they had bought. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage, while the Sun noted that the Black committee members were holding their ground despite "petty annoyances."

The Kansas City Sun carried the fullest coverage, reprinting the Post editorial on its front page, mocking the dynamite collection in an editorial brief, and headlining the church bombing "A Dastardly Outrage." Its church story was reprinted by the Metropolis Weekly Gazette on May 23 and by the Tulsa Star on May 24, the latter crediting the Sun.

The Topeka Plaindealer published an open letter to Mayor Cowgill on May 9 asking why any race should have a designated district and saying that when Black buyers moved into middle-class white areas "we hear of dynamite." The letter blamed the Kansas City Star for turning opinion against Black residents, and the Plaindealer reprinted it on June 6 with a note that several Black homes had been dynamited in the past few weeks. Farther away, the Cleveland Advocate listed the Kansas City dynamitings among examples under the heading "Creation of The Ghetto."

The Sun and the Metropolis Weekly Gazette dated the church blast to a Tuesday night, while the Tulsa Star's reprint of the same story said Thursday; the Sun, as the local original, is the better source.

reader.title: Kansas City housing dynamitings of 1919
bases: Beyond threats and protest meetings (A3, A4), Black papers reported dynamite attacks: several Black homes damaged (A7, A12) and a charge exploded under New Hope Baptist Church (A8).

Independent Black reports agree that Black homes in Kansas City were being dynamited in spring 1919 (A7 from Pearson's Magazine, A12 from the Topeka Plaindealer) amid white threats (A3, A4); the New Hope church blast itself rests on the Kansas City Sun alone (A8), reprinted in A10 and A11.

framing.detail: The Kansas City Sun headlined the church bombing 'A Dastardly Outrage', ran ironic editorial briefs on the dynamite collection, and reprinted the Kansas City Post's call for a biracial committee.

The Topeka Plaindealer addressed an open letter to Mayor Cowgill rejecting any designated district for Black buyers and blaming the Kansas City Star, reprinting it in June with a note that several Black homes had been dynamited.
The Cleveland Advocate placed the Kansas City dynamitings in a list of discriminations headed 'Creation of The Ghetto', drawn from Pearson's Magazine.
